title: Thin Film Interference
lead: The colors of a soap bubble or an oil slick come from light reflected from the top and bottom surfaces of a thin film. Whether the two reflected rays add or cancel depends on the thickness of the film, measured in wavelengths in the film, and on whether each reflection carries a half-wavelength shift. These ideas design non-reflective coatings and read the bands of an air wedge.
objectives: Discuss the rainbow formation by thin films.
summary_html:
• Thin film interference occurs between the light reflected from the top and bottom surfaces of a film. In addition to the path length difference, there can be a phase change.
  • When light reflects from a medium having an index of refraction greater than that of the medium in which it is traveling, a $180^\circ$ phase change (or a $\klam/2$ shift) occurs.
notes: Figure 27.32 is the soap bubble photograph of the chapter introduction (Figure 27.2) printed again under a new number, and it is kept here because the text points at it twice. In Example 27.7(b) the book prints $\frac{\lambda n}{2}$ where it means $\lambda_n/2$; the page carries it as printed. The keyed problem on an oil slick at a $45^\circ$ angle asks the reader to repeat an unkeyed problem, so its prompt states that problem’s data in place of the reference. Seven of the module’s fourteen problems have no keyed answer and are left out: the color of a 120-nm oil slick, the thinnest soap bubble that appears red, the three thicknesses of soapy water on Plexiglas, the thickest soap bubble that stays dark, the band spacing under a 0.100-mm hair, the soap bubble repeated at $45^\circ$, and the radar coating of Unreasonable Results.

figures.original_caption: These soap bubbles exhibit brilliant colors when exposed to sunlight. (credit: Scott Robinson, Flickr)

Light striking a thin film is partially reflected (ray 1) and partially refracted at the top surface. The refracted ray is partially reflected at the bottom surface and emerges as ray 2. These rays will interfere in a way that depends on the thickness of the film and the indices of refraction of the various media.
(a) The rainbow color bands are produced by thin film interference in the air between the two glass slides. (b) Schematic of the paths taken by rays in the wedge of air between the slides.

“Newton's rings” interference fringes are produced when two plano-convex lenses are placed together with their plane surfaces in contact. The rings are created by interference between the light reflected off the two surfaces as a result of a slight gap between them, indicating that these surfaces are not precisely plane but are slightly convex. (credit: Ulf Seifert, Wikimedia Commons)

exercises.prompt: Which of the following best describes the cause of thin film interference?

options: Light reflecting from a medium having an index of refraction less than that of the medium in which it is traveling.
Light reflecting from a medium having an index of refraction greater than that of the medium in which it is traveling.
Light changing its wavelength and speed after reflection.
Light reflecting from the top and bottom surfaces of a film.
answer.hint: Ask which two waves meet and interfere when you see the colors of a film.

exercises.prompt: A film of magnesium fluoride (n = 1.38) is used to coat a glass camera lens (n = 1.52). If the thickness of the film is 105 nm, calculate the wavelength of visible light that will have the most limited reflection.

answer.solution: Both reflections carry a $\klam/2$ shift, since the light goes from air to magnesium fluoride at the top surface and from magnesium fluoride to glass at the bottom one, so the shifts cancel. The reflection is most limited when the extra path $2\ktfilm$ is half a wavelength in the film, $2\ktfilm = \klamn/2$ with $\klamn = \klam/n$. Solve for the vacuum wavelength, $\klam = 4n\ktfilm$, enter $n = 1.38$ and $\ktfilm = 105\;\text{nm}$, and check that the result lies in the visible range, as Example 27.6 does for 550-nm light.

exercises.prompt: What effect does increasing the wedge angle have on the spacing of interference fringes? If the wedge angle is too large, fringes are not observed. Why?

answer.solution: Neighboring dark bands lie where the air is half a wavelength thicker, so a steeper wedge reaches that extra thickness over a shorter distance and the fringes crowd closer together. If the wedge angle is too large, the fringes become so close that the eye cannot separate them, and the thickness soon becomes many wavelengths, where slight changes in the angle of incidence change the path length difference enough to wash the pattern out.

exercises.prompt: How is the difference in paths taken by two originally in-phase light waves related to whether they interfere constructively or destructively? How can this be affected by reflection? By refraction?

answer.solution: Two waves that start in phase interfere constructively when their path length difference is a whole number of wavelengths, so that crest meets crest, and destructively when it is a half-integral number of wavelengths, so that crest meets trough. Reflection from a medium of greater index adds a $\klam/2$ shift to one wave, which turns constructive into destructive and the reverse. Refraction into a medium of index $n$ shortens the wavelength to $\klamn = \klam/n$, so a given path inside the medium holds more wavelengths and the path difference must be counted in the wavelength of the medium.

exercises.prompt: Is there a phase change in the light reflected from either surface of a contact lens floating on a person’s tear layer? The index of refraction of the lens is about 1.5, and its top surface is dry.

answer.solution: Apply the rule at each surface. At the dry top surface light goes from air, $n = 1.00$, toward the lens, $n \approx 1.5$, which has the greater index, so the reflected light has a $\klam/2$ shift. At the bottom surface light inside the lens reflects from the tear layer, which is mostly water with $n \approx 1.33$, a smaller index, so there is no phase change there.

exercises.prompt: In placing a sample on a microscope slide, a glass cover is placed over a water drop on the glass slide. Light incident from above can reflect from the top and bottom of the glass cover and from the glass slide below the water drop. At which surfaces will there be a phase change in the reflected light?

answer.solution: Compare the index on each side of every surface, taking glass as about 1.52 and water as 1.333. At the top of the cover, light in air reflects from glass of greater index, so there is a phase change. At the bottom of the cover, light in glass reflects from water of smaller index, so there is none. At the top of the slide, light in water reflects from glass of greater index, so there is a phase change again.

exercises.prompt: Answer the above question if the fluid between the two pieces of crown glass is carbon disulfide.

answer.solution: Carbon disulfide has an index of about 1.63, greater than that of crown glass, about 1.52. At the top of the cover, light in air reflects from glass, so there is still a phase change. At the bottom of the cover, light in glass now reflects from a fluid of greater index, so there is a phase change there too. At the top of the slide, light in carbon disulfide reflects from glass of smaller index, so there is no phase change.

exercises.prompt: While contemplating the food value of a slice of ham, you notice a rainbow of color reflected from its moist surface. Explain its origin.

answer.solution: The moist surface carries a thin film of water, and possibly of fat, whose thickness varies from place to place. Light reflected from the top and bottom surfaces of the film interferes, and at each thickness a different wavelength interferes constructively. White light therefore reflects as a band of different colors wherever the thickness changes, as in a soap bubble. Some of the color may also come from the regular structure of the meat’s fibers acting like a diffraction grating.

exercises.prompt: An inventor notices that a soap bubble is dark at its thinnest and realizes that destructive interference is taking place for all wavelengths. How could she use this knowledge to make a non-reflective coating for lenses that is effective at all wavelengths? That is, what limits would there be on the index of refraction and thickness of the coating? How might this be impractical?

answer.solution: The bubble is dark at every wavelength because only one of its two reflections carries a $\klam/2$ shift and the path length difference is negligible. A coating would need the same. An index greater than that of air but smaller than that of the glass would shift both reflections. The coating would instead need an index greater than that of the lens, so that only the top reflection shifts, and a thickness much smaller than the wavelength, a few tens of nanometers at most. Such a coating is hard to make and to keep uniform. The two reflections would also have to be about equally strong to cancel fully, and a high-index layer on top reflects strongly on its own if its thickness is not exactly right.

exercises.prompt: A non-reflective coating like the one described in Example 27.6 works ideally for a single wavelength and for perpendicular incidence. What happens for other wavelengths and other incident directions? Be specific.

answer.solution: The coating is a quarter of a wavelength thick in the film for one wavelength only. For shorter or longer wavelengths the extra path $2\ktfilm$ is no longer exactly half a wavelength in the film, so the two reflections cancel only in part and some light reflects. The ends of the spectrum, violet and red, reflect most, which is why coated lenses look faintly purple. For light arriving at an angle, the ray inside the film travels a longer, slanted path. The path length difference changes, the best-cancelled wavelength shifts, and the coating works less well.

exercises.prompt: Why is it much more difficult to see interference fringes for light reflected from a thick piece of glass than from a thin film? Would it be easier if monochromatic light were used?

answer.solution: In thick glass the path length difference is many thousands of wavelengths, so a tiny change in thickness, wavelength or angle of incidence moves the pattern from constructive to destructive. In white light every wavelength has its own pattern, and at such a large path difference they overlap and average to an even brightness; different angles from an extended source also blur the fringes. Monochromatic light removes the mixing of wavelengths and so helps, but the fringes still shift greatly with small changes in angle, and ordinary light is not coherent over such long paths, so they remain hard to see.

exercises.prompt: A soap bubble is 100 nm thick and illuminated by white light incident perpendicular to its surface. What wavelength and color of visible light is most constructively reflected, assuming the same index of refraction as water?

answer.hint: Only the top reflection is shifted, so constructive interference needs $2\ktfilm = \klamn/2$ with $\klamn = \klam/n$.

exercises.prompt: Calculate the minimum thickness of an oil slick on water that appears blue when illuminated by white light perpendicular to its surface. Take the blue wavelength to be 470 nm and the index of refraction of oil to be 1.40.

answer.hint: Air to oil is shifted and oil to water is not, so the thinnest constructive film has $2\ktfilm = \klamn/2$.

exercises.prompt: A film of soapy water ($n=1.33$) on top of a plastic cutting board has a thickness of 233 nm. What color is most strongly reflected if it is illuminated perpendicular to its surface?

answer.hint: Take the plastic to have a greater index than the soapy water, so both reflections are shifted and constructive interference needs $2\ktfilm$ to be a whole number of wavelengths in the film.

exercises.prompt: Suppose you have a lens system that is to be used primarily for 700-nm red light. What is the second thinnest coating of magnesium fluoride that would be non-reflective for this wavelength? Refer to Table 25.1 for the index of refraction.

answer.hint: As in Example 27.6 both reflections are shifted; the second destructive thickness has $2\ktfilm = 3\klamn/2$.

exercises.prompt: A film of oil on water will appear dark when it is very thin, because the path length difference becomes small compared with the wavelength of light and there is a phase shift at the top surface. If it becomes dark when the path length difference is less than one-fourth the wavelength, what is the thickest the oil can be and appear dark at all visible wavelengths? Oil has an index of refraction of 1.40.

answer.hint: Set $2\ktfilm$ equal to one-fourth of the shortest visible wavelength in the oil, taking 380 nm in a vacuum.

exercises.prompt: Figure 27.34 shows two 7.50-cm-long glass slides illuminated by pure 589-nm wavelength light incident perpendicularly. The top slide touches the bottom slide at one end and rests on some debris at the other end, forming a wedge of air. How thick is the debris, if the dark bands are 1.00 mm apart?

answer.hint: From one dark band to the next the air grows $\klam/2$ thicker; count the bands along the whole slide.

exercises.prompt: An oil slick on water is 120 nm thick and illuminated by white light, and its index of refraction is 1.40. What color does the oil appear (what is the most constructively reflected wavelength) if the light is incident at a $45^\circ$ angle?

answer.solution: The oil film will appear black, since the reflected light is not in the visible part of the spectrum.
